Use `v-model` on your component in the parent, and in the child use `defineModel()` (recommended in Vue 3.4+) to create a two-way binding:

```vue
<!-- Parent -->
<MyInput v-model="text" />

<!-- MyInput.vue -->
<script setup>
const model = defineModel()
</script>

<template>
  <input v-model="model" />
</template>
```

Behind the scenes, Vue uses a `modelValue` prop and an `update:modelValue` event. The parent’s `v-model="text"` is compiled to a prop binding and an event listener that updates `text`.

In Vue 3.4+, use `defineModel()` in your input component, then bind the returned ref to the native input:

```vue
<script setup>
const model = defineModel()
</script>

<template>
  <input v-model="model" />
</template>
```

A parent can then use `<MyInput v-model="value" />`. Behind the scenes, Vue uses a `modelValue` prop and an `update:modelValue` event. Before Vue 3.4, you can implement that pair with `defineProps(['modelValue'])` and `defineEmits(['update:modelValue'])`.

Use `v-model` on your component, and in Vue 3.4+ use `defineModel()` in the child to create the two-way binding:


Vue tracks reactive object properties by intercepting property access through a proxy. Copying or destructuring a property into a local variable disconnects that variable from the proxy: reading or changing the local variable no longer triggers the proxy’s tracking or update mechanisms.

For a primitive property, the local variable is just a separate value. If it holds an object, mutating that object can still be reactive, but reassigning the local variable itself is not.

Destructuring a property copies its current value into a local variable. After that, reads and writes to the local variable no longer go through the reactive object’s proxy, so Vue can’t track or trigger updates through that binding. This is especially true for primitive values such as numbers.

Keep using the property through the reactive object (for example, `state.count`) to retain the connection.
